lead: Helping people find their place at Scoot
intro: A career portal for people who know the role they want, and those who don’t yet.
challengeTitle: Not everyone arrives with a job title
challenge:
Scoot was growing fast and needed a career portal that could attract new talent. I designed it end to end, within Scoot’s existing design system, adding components where it had gaps.

The brief assumed visitors already knew which job they wanted. Interviews and data from the old portal said otherwise. Some searched for a specific role. Some wanted to know where their skills fit. Some were just curious about working at Scoot.

I designed the homepage, job search, culture and brand values, internships and staff profiles. This case study focuses on job search.
researchIntro: With extra hands from the team, we interviewed around 30 people. Their answers fell into three groups, each with a different question to answer before applying.

personas.title: Flight crew candidates
personas.alt: Scoot illustration of a pilot and cabin crew member
personas.question: What does it take to join the crew?
personas.need: Clear recruitment steps, training requirements and a feel for team culture.

personas.title: Office-role candidates
personas.alt: Scoot illustration representing an office-role candidate
personas.question: Where does my experience fit?
personas.need: Departments, relevant roles and room to grow, especially when coming from another industry.

personas.title: Curious visitors
personas.alt: Scoot illustration representing a curious visitor
personas.question: Is there anything here for me?
personas.need: An overview of roles, without choosing a job title first.

designTitle: Search by role, or by skills
designIntro: Most visitors were on their phones, so I designed mobile first, then adapted for desktop. Search has two routes: keywords for people who know their role, skills for people who don’t yet.

decisions.title: Keyword search
decisions.body: For people who know their role. Keyword search sits at the top of the homepage. Results open on the job board, where filters for location, experience, department and employment type narrow the list.

decisions.title: Skills search
decisions.body: For people who aren’t sure where they fit. Scoot hires for many entry-level roles and welcomes people who don’t yet know how their skills apply. Instead of a job title, they pick skills Scoot is looking for.

decisions.title: Why five skills
decisions.body:
Five core skills are enough to narrow down the options. It’s a search, not a CV, so there’s no need to list everything.

Each job is tagged with up to five core skills too, so the two sets match directly. Skills combine like a boolean search.

decisions.title: Fewer dead ends
decisions.body: Search understands related skills: typing “analysis” also suggests analytics skills. This cuts down searches that return few or no jobs.

testingTitle: Why the old career finder didn’t work
testing:
The previous site had two dropdowns, called career finders: one for internships, one for full-time corporate roles. Feedback was that they weren’t useful.

The internship finder let people pick an area of interest. That suggested a matching internship existed. Being on the list didn’t mean a role was open.

The corporate finder only worked if people already knew what they were looking for. That shut out candidates early in their careers, who could fit a range of roles.

Scoot is growing fast, and a sizeable share of its roles suit entry-level and junior candidates. Research showed we needed more room for younger people looking for an opportunity. Skills search grew out of the career finders to fill that gap.
